newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-Sedgwick to reflect industry woes.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Sedgwick to reflect industry woes.

text.p: Sedgwick Group, the British based insurance broker, is expected to underline the difficulties of overcapacity and falling rates faced by the industry when it reports 1996 results on Tuesday.

Those problems have already been highlighted this week by Willis Corroon who said that rates were continuing to decline almost universally. The recent strength in sterling which reduced Willis profits by 3.1 million stg is a further worry, prompting a warning from Willis that if sustained it was likely to damage 1997 results.
Analysts forecast Sedgwick will report pre-tax profits of between 92 and 98.5 million stg. Consensus estimates of 94.5 are some five percent ahead of last year's 90.1 million stg.
The dividend is expected to be maintained at 6.5 pence per share.
Consulting and employee benefits account for some 22 percent of revenues and Sedgwick's geographic and business mix makes it more diversified than Willis, said one analyst.
It is also ahead in moving to a 50/50 commissions/fees basis of revenues which should improve the durability of its earnings, he said.
In November Sedgwick reported nine month pre-tax profits of 80.4 million stg, slightly ahead of analyst forecasts.
Growth areas then were in the Asia-Pacific region and Sedgwick Noble Lowndes.
At the time, Sedgwick chief executive Sax Riley highlighted the resilient performance despite difficult market conditions and was upbeat about prospects for the rest of the year.
The group's operational strategy has been focused on lessening the group's dependence on the underwriting cycle by increasing fee-earning consultancy business.
It has also concentrated on broadening its business base and the need to keep a tight control on costs.
Toward the end of last year Sedgwick was at the centre of speculation that it could merge with a U.S. rival, though the company has consistently refused to comment on the rumours.

New York-based Marsh & Mclennan was repeatedly suggested as a partner, a move that would re-secure the U.S. company's position as the world's largest broker after Aon's $1.23 million takeover of Alexander & Alexander.
Riley heightened speculation in August when he suggested a merger with another broker was possible and that there was room for only three or four big players in the insurance broking market.
But analysts expect Sedgwick to restate its commitment, in the short term at least, to its independence.
"I expect Sedgwick will admit that A&A makes things a bit different but that they will say that they can soldier on as an independent," said one.
